name: Rift
headline: A coding agent that treats local models as first-class citizens.
standfirst: Rift is a Rust terminal coding agent built around small binaries, local inference, explicit context control and failure recovery.
evidence: Repository, README, benchmark notes and public project material. Toolglass has not installed or run Rift.

body.heading: What is it?
paragraphs: Rift is a terminal coding agent written in Rust with Ollama and OpenAI-compatible local servers treated as primary targets rather than compatibility afterthoughts. The project also exposes headless JSON output, a VS Code bridge, a desktop shell and a worktree-based parallel mode called WarpDrive.

body.heading: Why did Radar notice it?
paragraphs: Most coding agents assume a large hosted model and abundant context. Rift is interesting because it designs around the opposite constraints: local models, finite context, unreliable tool calling and the need to see when truncation or repetition is happening.

Its benchmark claims are unusually concrete for a tiny project: same-model task suites, prompt-token accounting and recorded traces rather than a vague 'fast' badge. Those numbers remain project claims until independently reproduced.

body.heading: What's the catch?
paragraphs: The project is very small and moving quickly. Its strongest performance claims come from its own benchmark harness, and local-model reliability is highly sensitive to model choice, prompt format and server behaviour. Toolglass has not reproduced the comparisons or tested its recovery paths.

body.heading: Who might want it?
paragraphs: Developers running Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio or llama.cpp who want an agent that assumes local inference is normal, plus people who care about prompt-token budgets and transparent failure handling more than ecosystem polish.

verdict: One of the more technically specific local-first coding-agent projects Radar has seen; promising precisely because it attacks the boring failure modes instead of pretending they do not exist.
nextStep: Re-run its published task suite against the same local model and compare token counts, completion rate and wall time with one established agent.
